Two distinct magnetization components, C1 and C2, were identified. C1 is interpreted as a depositional or post-depositional remanent magnetiza - tion carried by detrital pseudo-single domain (PSD) magnetite, while the C2 component is a thermochemical remanent magnetization carried by fine authigenic single domain (SD)–PSD magnetite. The deposition paleo - latitude provided by C1 is 33.3° ± 3.2°, which gives an initial quantitative approximation of the paleolatitude for the underlying Mari- noan Ghaub diamictites. The thickness of the Keilberg Member cap dolostone is anoma - lously high for the paleolatitude calculated with C1, which suggests that other factors besides the influence of the paleolatitude on carbonate oversaturation may have influ - enced the sedimentary production of cap dolostones and the overall thick

indicative of low paleolatitudes, have been documented within a considerable number of glacial depos- its from both the Sturtian and Marinoan glacia- tions across various cratons (e.g., Evans, 2000; Trindade and Macouin, 2007; Hoffman and Li, 2009; Evans and Raub, 2011). However, despite the abundance of such records, highly reliable poles derived directly from glacial units remain very limited in number. Evans and Raub’s com- prehensive review in 2011 highlighted that merely two glacial units present robust data displaying this characteristic. These units are the Marinoan Elatina Formation in Southern Australia (Schmidt and Williams, 1995; Sohl et al., 1999) and the Marinoan Nantuo Forma - tion in South China (Zhang and Piper, 1997; Zhang et al., 2013). Nonetheless, a substantial body of “moderately reliable” paleomagnetic evidence directly sourced from glacial deposits, combined with high-quality data inferred from volcanic units temporally associated with glacial periods (e.g., Franklin Large Igneous Province data from Denyszyn et al., 2009), robustly sup- ports the occurrence of SBE events and the low paleolatitude positioning of many Cryogenian glacial deposits (Evans and Raub, 2011). Importantly, if such a phenomenon proves to be primary and global, the wide - spread occurrence of these stratigraphically compressed reversals would support the pre- cise temporal correlation between Marinoan cap dolostones. The first popula - tion consists of larger, less coercive magnetite, presumably exhibiting a PSD/MD structure (Figs. 8 and 10), and is more prominent in the carbonate matrix of samples bearing the C1 component. The second population consists of finer magnetite with an SD/PSD structure (<2 μm), which is primarily, but not exclusively, found in conjunction with clays and micas in samples carrying C2. 5. INTRODUCTION During the Cryogenian period (ca. 720–635 Ma), two instances occurred in which glacial deposits were overlain by the sudden and mas- sive precipitation of thick carbonate sequences referred to as cap carbonates. Carbonate forma- tions typically develop in low-latitude regions of the planet under warm aquatic conditions (Opdyke and Wilkinson, 1990; Millero, 1979; Jiang et al., 2015). Hence, the presence of both glacial and carbonate rocks indicates a climatic state markedly distinct from any observed dur- ing the Phanerozoic eon (Hoffman et al., 1998). Corroborated by an

tud - ies, particularly when considering factors like regional extension (i.e., multiple sampled sec - tions) and stratigraphic control. Noteworthy results indicating relatively low paleolatitudes (<40°) have been obtained in different loca - tions, including Brazil (Mirassol d’Oeste cap dolostone; Trindade et al., 2003), Oman (Hadash cap dolostone; Kilner et al., 2005), Southern Australia (Nuccaleena cap carbonate; Schmidt et al., 2009), and South China (Doushantuo cap carbonate; Zhang et al., 2015). However, the reliability of these paleomagnetic data is problematic, as only the Nuccaleena Formation has undergone a convincing fold test, while the remaining units lack such tests or exhibit folding events that are considerably more recent than the cap formation itself. Importantly, all of these cap carbonates exhibit more than one geomagnetic reversal, primarily concentrated in their basal cap dolo- stone levels, which corresponds to the transgres- sive system tract (TST) sequence. This phenom- enon has sparked interest due to the potential for establishing correlations and investigating synchronicity among these time polarities, and also prompts questions about the timing of depo- sition, assuming a knowledge of the duration required for these reversals to occur. I

sequence culminates in the highstand dolostone, which is initially allodapic with thin layers like the underlying limestone, and evolves into more massive grainstone that becomes coarser upward, and ends with a highly silicified expo- sure surface. This surface is overlain by numer- ous tepee cycles of the lower Elandshoek For - mation (Hoffman, 2011). Sampling was conducted along the Hoanib River escarpments in northern Namibia, within the inner platform zone of the Otavi Group (Figs. 1 and 2). This zone was chosen for paleo- magnetic sampling due to its expected higher detrital input, which enhances the probability of obtaining a primary direction. Our focus was on the Keilberg dolostones and immediately over- lying limestone, where we aimed to capture a paleomagnetic direction closely related to gla - ciogenic rocks and detect potential reversals near the contact, analogous to other cap carbonates. Two sections (A and B) from a synform with a NE–SW axial plane were collected for a fold test (Fig. 2). The orientation and position of the fold suggest that it resulted from the main Kao- koan folding phase, which occurred between 580 Ma and 570 Ma (Goscombe et al., 2005; Goscombe et al., 2018). In this study, we examined the Maieberg Formation cap carbonates in northern Namibia (Congo craton), which overlay the Ghaub For- mation diamictites—a cornerstone of the SBE hypothesis (Hoffman et al., 1998; Hoffman and Schrag, 2002; Hoffman et al., 2021)—yet lack paleomagnetic data. INTRODUCTION During the Cryogenian period (ca. 720–635 Ma), two instances occurred in which glacial deposits were overlain by the sudden and mas- sive precipitation of thick carbonate sequences referred to as cap carbonates. Carbonate forma- tions typically develop in low-latitude regions of the planet under warm aquatic conditions (Opdyke and Wilkinson, 1990; Millero, 1979; Jiang et al., 2015). Hence, the presence of both glacial and carbonate rocks indicates a climatic state markedly distinct from any observed dur- ing the Phanerozoic eon (Hoffman et al., 1998). Corroborated by an

However, the reliability of these paleomagnetic data is problematic, as only the Nuccaleena Formation has undergone a convincing fold test, while the remaining units lack such tests or exhibit folding events that are considerably more recent than the cap formation itself. Importantly, all of these cap carbonates exhibit more than one geomagnetic reversal, primarily concentrated in their basal cap dolo- stone levels, which corresponds to the transgres- sive system tract (TST) sequence. This phenom- enon has sparked interest due to the potential for establishing correlations and investigating synchronicity among these time polarities, and also prompts questions about the timing of depo- sition, assuming a knowledge of the duration required for these reversals to occur. Factors such as ocean warming, thermal expansion, and local glacio-isostatic adjustments imply extended marine transgressions beyond the deglaciation period. Still, magnetostrati - graphic estimates for postglacial transgres - sive sequences require longer time scales by a factor of five or more. Thus, the conflict aris- ing between estimates derived from paleo - magnetic data and the constraints imposed by climate physics underscores uncertainties regarding an unconventional field state or a remanence acquisition mechanism within these cap carbonates that is not fully under- stood. Although the chronostratigraphic age of the Chuanlinggou Formation that hosts the Xuanlong-type ironstone is well-constrained (~1.64 Ga, Fig. 1 c; details in Section 2 ), the miner - alization age of the hematite is unknown, as described above. Therefore, we conducted a study integrating paleomagnetic and rock magnetic methods, and SEM observations and EDS analysis on the late Paleo - proterozoic Xuanlong-type ironstone. Our objectives were to determine the mineralization age of the hematite in the Xuanlong-type ironstone and to evaluate whether hematite was the primary Fe-bearing mineral. Overall, we aimed to develop a new approach to evaluate the primary Fe-bearing minerals in iron formations and to further explore the pale - oenvironmental signals preserved in the Xuanlong-type ironstone. 2. The Jiezha Group refers to a set of clastic and carbonate sediments that overlie the Upper Permian strata with an angular unconformity. This group, from bottom to top, includes the Jiapila, Bolila, and Bagong formations. Lithologi- cally, the Jiapila Formation consists mainly of clastic rocks bearing andesite and limestone ( Fig. 2b). The Bolila Formation is composed of gray micrite, calcite dolomite which interbed with sandstone. The Bagong Formation primarily consists of quartz sandstone and carbonaceous shale interbedded with limestone lenses, bears coal seams (streaks) ( Fig. 2c). These three formations conform with one another sequentially. The paleontological assemblage, such as Quemocuomegalodon orientus-Neomegalodon cornutus from the Jiapila Formation, H. superbescens, H. disperseinsecta from the Bolila and Bagong formations, are recognized in these strata, and indicate a Norian age (Late Triassic) ( Tang et al., 201 1). The Jiezha Group is unconformably overlain by the MiddleeUpper Jurassic Yanshiping Group in the sampling area (e.g., Li et al., 2012 ). carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Accepted 6 May 2019 Available online 21 May 2019 Handling Editor: Wenjiao Xiao Keywords: Northern Qiangtang block Paleomagnetism Plate tectonics Tethys ocean Tibetan plateau Triassic abstract As one of the pivotal Gondwana ederived blocks, the kinematic history of the northern Qiangtang Block (in the Tibetan Plateau) remains unclear, mainly because quantitative paleomagnetic data to determine the paleoposition are sparse. Thus, for this study, we collected 226 samples (17 sites) from Triassic sedimentary rocks in the Raggyorcaka and Tuotuohe areas of the northern Qiangtang Block (NQB). Stepwise demagnetization isolated high temperature/ ﬁeld components from the samples. Both Early and Late Triassic datasets passed ﬁeld tests at a 99% con ﬁdence level and were proved to be primary origins. Paleopoles were calculated to be at 24.9 N and 216.5 E with A95 ¼ 8.2 (N ¼ 8) for the Early Triassic dataset, and at 68.1 N, 179.9 Ew i t hA95 ¼ 5.6 (N ¼ 37) for the Late Triassic, the latter being combined with a coeval volcanic dataset published previously. These paleopoles correspond to paleolatitudes of 14.3 S/C6 8.2 and 29.9 N/C6 5.6 , respectively. Combining previously published results, we reconstructed a three-stage northward drift process for the NQB. (1) The northern Qiangtang Block was located in the subtropical part of the southern hemisphere until the Early Triassic; (2) thereafter, the block rapidly drifted northward

The Jiezha Group refers to a set of clastic and carbonate sediments that overlie the Upper Permian strata with an angular unconformity. This group, from bottom to top, includes the Jiapila, Bolila, and Bagong formations. Lithologi- cally, the Jiapila Formation consists mainly of clastic rocks bearing andesite and limestone ( Fig. 2b). The Bolila Formation is composed of gray micrite, calcite dolomite which interbed with sandstone. The Bagong Formation primarily consists of quartz sandstone and carbonaceous shale interbedded with limestone lenses, bears coal seams (streaks) ( Fig. 2c). These three formations conform with one another sequentially. The paleontological assemblage, such as Quemocuomegalodon orientus-Neomegalodon cornutus from the Jiapila Formation, H. superbescens, H. disperseinsecta from the Bolila and Bagong formations, are recognized in these strata, and indicate a Norian age (Late Triassic) ( Tang et al., 201 1). The Jiezha Group is unconformably overlain by the MiddleeUpper Jurassic Yanshiping Group in the sampling area (e.g., Li et al., 2012 ). carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Accepted 6 May 2019 Available online 21 May 2019 Handling Editor: Wenjiao Xiao Keywords: Northern Qiangtang block Paleomagnetism Plate tectonics Tethys ocean Tibetan plateau Triassic abstract As one of the pivotal Gondwana ederived blocks, the kinematic history of the northern Qiangtang Block (in the Tibetan Plateau) remains unclear, mainly because quantitative paleomagnetic data to determine the paleoposition are sparse. Thus, for this study, we collected 226 samples (17 sites) from Triassic sedimentary rocks in the Raggyorcaka and Tuotuohe areas of the northern Qiangtang Block (NQB). Stepwise demagnetization isolated high temperature/ ﬁeld components from the samples. Both Early and Late Triassic datasets passed ﬁeld tests at a 99% con ﬁdence level and were proved to be primary origins. Paleopoles were calculated to be at 24.9 N and 216.5 E with A95 ¼ 8.2 (N ¼ 8) for the Early Triassic dataset, and at 68.1 N, 179.9 Ew i t hA95 ¼ 5.6 (N ¼ 37) for the Late Triassic, the latter being combined with a coeval volcanic dataset published previously. These paleopoles correspond to paleolatitudes of 14.3 S/C6 8.2 and 29.9 N/C6 5.6 , respectively. Combining previously published results, we reconstructed a three-stage northward drift process for the NQB. (1) The northern Qiangtang Block was located in the subtropical part of the southern hemisphere until the Early Triassic; (2) thereafter, the block rapidly drifted northward

Lithologi- cally, the Jiapila Formation consists mainly of clastic rocks bearing andesite and limestone ( Fig. 2b). The Bolila Formation is composed of gray micrite, calcite dolomite which interbed with sandstone. The Bagong Formation primarily consists of quartz sandstone and carbonaceous shale interbedded with limestone lenses, bears coal seams (streaks) ( Fig. 2c). These three formations conform with one another sequentially. The Jiezha Group is unconformably overlain by the MiddleeUpper Jurassic Yanshiping Group in the sampling area (e.g., Li et al., 2012 ). ABSTRACT The paleogeographic positions of the North China craton (NCC) during the late Mesoproterozoic to early Neo - proterozoic are important to understand the supercontinent evolution. However, the published paleomagnetic results for this period were mainly obtained from the Liaodong – Xuhuai regions, situated along the eastern margin of the craton. They would further benefit from the data from more regions. In this study, we present the new paleomagnetic results obtained from the carbonate rocks of the upper part of the Jingeryu Formation (Fm) in the eastern Heibei Province, Yanliao basin, located in the interior of the NCC. Stepwise demagnetization revealed two distinct paleomagnetic remanence components. The low-stability component is likely a viscous magnetic remanence acquired in the recent geomagnetic field. Ninety-four samples retained a high-stability component, which is dual-polarity and characterized by notably steep inclinations, positioning the paleomag - netic pole at 45.6 ◦ N, 139.6 ◦ E ( dp / dm = 8.7 ◦ /8.9 ◦ ). The primary origin of the remanent magnetization is supported by positive fold and reversal tests, as well as the new pole ’ s distinctiveness from the younger NCC poles. The Jingeryu pole overlaps (at the 95 % confidence level) with poles from the lower pa

e North American Midcontinent Rift (MCR) volcanic rocks ( Swanson-Hysell et al., 2019 ). However, these NCC data are predominantly from the eastern margin of the craton. High-quality paleomagnetic data from the interior of the craton would therefore benefit the reconstruction models. The Jingeryu Fm, characterized by extensive platform-facies car - bonate deposition in the Yanliao basin within the interior of the NCC, has been suggested being correlative with the Nanfen Fm based on their lithologic similarities and the stratigraphic sequence (e.g., Kuang et al., 2023; Su, 2016; Xing et al., 1996 ). In this study, we mainly report the paleomagnetic results newly obtained from the upper part of the Jin - geryu Fm, and offer new insights into refining the regional stratigraphic correlation scheme and global paleocontinental reconstructions, based on an synthesis with the global paleomagnetic database. 2. However, high-quality Middle Jurassic paleomagnetic data from the Lhasa terrane are limited in number. Abstract The drift history of the Lhasa terrane is crucial for understanding the tectonic evolution of Tethyan Oceans and Jurassic true polar wander. However, high-quality Middle Jurassic paleomagnetic data from the Lhasa terrane are limited in number. Here we report a combined paleomagnetic and geochronologic study on the Yeba Formation volcanic rocks, dated at ∼170 Ma, from the Lhasa terrane. Robust field and reversal tests indicate that the characteristic remanent magnetizations are primary. Our results provide a reliable Middle Jurassic (∼170 Ma) paleopole at 29.8°N, 180.7°E with A95 = 5.7° and a paleolatitude of 14.4 ± 5.7°N for the Lhasa area. Compared with previous paleomagnetic and geologic evidence, we propose that the Meso-Tethys Ocean probably began to close in the eastern part at ∼168 Ma and that the Lhasa terrane underwent a ∼2,900 km southward “monster shift” during the Late Jurassic. ntary interlayers (Figure S1 in Supporting Information S1). Strata of sites YB1−5, YB6−10, and YB11−35 dip ∼52° toward the northwest, ∼82° toward to the north-northeast, and ∼68−84° toward the southwest, respectively (Figure 1c; Table S1 in Supporting Information S1). Generally, each site contains at least 8 core samples collected using a portable gasoline-powered drill. All core samples were oriented using both a magnetic compass and a Sun compass, and the declination differences between the two oriented methods are less than 3°. Fifteen core samples from independent cobbles within the conglomerate interlayer (YBC) were drilled for the conglomerate test (Figure S1d in Supporting Information S1). In addition, two fresh volcanic block samples for zircon U-Pb dating were collected from sites YB1 and YB22, respectively (Figures S1a and S1c in Supporting Information S1). Plain Language Summary The Central Asian Orogenic Belt (CAOB) is the largest accretionary orogenic belt on earth since begin of the Phanerozoic. Since the Late Paleozoic, two prominent sutures, namely the Hegenshan and Solonker sutures, have played crucial roles in the tectonic evolution of the eastern CAOB, as they were associated with the closure of the Paleo-Asian Ocean (PAO). The timing of the formation of the Hegenshan suture, however, remains ambiguous due to the lack of reliable paleomagnetic data. In this study, we present accurately dated paleomagnetic constraints on the paleogeographic position of the Mongolia Block (MOB), located on the northern side of the Hegenshan suture, at ∼250 Ma. By combining high-quality Late Permian–Early Triassic paleomagnetic data with geological evidence, we propose a new reconstruction that suggests the near-simultaneous closure of both the Hegenshan and Solonker oceans around 250 Ma. This significant event marks the final disappearance of the PAO and represents a fundamental stage in the establis

Therefore, high-quality paleomagnetic data from the MOB are still required to constrain its paleogeographic location during the Middle Permian–Middle Triassic. In this paper, we present new paleomagnetic and geochronological data for andesites from the upper Gunbayn Formation (Fm) of southeastern Mongolia, located in the MOB, with an age of ∼250 Ma. Our new data, combined with previously published Middle Permian–Middle Triassic paleomagnetic data and geological information, yield important insights into the paleogeographic relationship between the MOB and the XSB. Furthermore, we constrain the spatiotemporal evolution of the PAO, which played a key role in the formation of the CAOB. 2. In this paper, we present paleomag - netic results obtained from the Middle Perm- ian limestones and Upper Permian volcanic rocks in the Tanggula area, aiming to provide precise constraints on the NQB kinematics during the geodynamic evolution of the Te - thys realm. In this paper, we present paleomag - netic results obtained from the Middle Perm- ian limestones and Upper Permian volcanic rocks in the Tanggula area, aiming to provide precise constraints on the NQB kinematics during the geodynamic evolution of the Te - thys realm. The conspicuous inclination discrepancies in the Upper Cretaceous redbed paleomagnetic data may be explained by some factors such as: (1) insufficient averaging of geomagnetic paleos - ecular variation (e.g., Deenen et al., 2011; Vaes et al., 2021); (2) a secondary chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) recorded in the redbeds that partially or completely overprints the DRM (e.g., Kodama, 2012; Jiang et al., 2015, 2022); (3) the distortional strains should be taken seriously when the remanence directions are obtained from two limbs of folds (Cogné et al., 1991; Kanamatsu and Herrero-Bervera, 2006; Kligfield et al., 1983); (4) the depositional and/or compaction of redbeds may result in the ChRM inclination shallowing (e.g., Tauxe and Kent, 2004; Tan et al., 2010; Ding et al., 2015); and (5) the strata may not have been horizontal at the time of magnetization because of unidentified syntectonic growth strata (Gilder et al., 2001; Sato et al., 2011; Tong et al., 2019; Bian et al., 2020; Bian and Yang, 2021; Wang et al., 2022). As the Turpan- Hami block is mainly covered by Mesozoic and Cenozoic sedimentary layers ( Fig. 1D), our sampling was conducted along its northern margin, where Upper Paleozoic strata outcrops are abundant. The oldest strata exposed in this region are Ordovician, regarded as a folded base- ment mainly consisting of metamorphic lavas, clastic rocks, and marbles. Probably related to a late Caledonian orogenic event, Silurian strata are absent (Xu et al., 2014). From bottom to top, the late Paleozoic strata in the northern margin of the Turpan-Hami block are composed of the Middle Devonian Dananhu Formation (D2 d), Lower Carboniferous Jiangbasitao Formation (C1j), Upper Carboniferous Qijiaojing Forma- tion (C2q) and Julideneng Formation (C2j), and Lower Permian Kulai Formation (P1 k). The critical values (2.12 and 2.94) were smaller than the ratio of the preci - sion parameter (ks/kg = 5.18), indicating that the ChRM directions were acquired before folding. Second, the correlation test was also positive at 95% and 99% confidence intervals (McFadden, 1990). The test value in geographic coordinates (ξ1,g = 8.448) was larger than the critical values (3.865 and 5.378), whereas the tilt-corrected test value (ξ1,s) was equal to 1.492, suggesting that there is no correlation between bedding attitudes and the mean direction. ibetan Plateau Earth System, Environment and Resources (TPESER), Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Abstract The Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision closed the Meso‐Tethys Ocean, but the exact timing of this event remains hotly debated. Overall, these geological observations indicate that the Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision likely occurred during ca. 133– 116 Ma (Figure 3b ). Our paleomagnetic analysis reveals that the Cretaceous standstill of western Lhasa following rapid northward motion happened after ∼ 132 Ma. Future research focusing on high‐quality paleopoles from Upper Jurassic‐Lowest Cretaceous units both in western Lhasa and Qiangtang will further refine the processes involved in the evolution of the Meso‐ Tethys. The comparison of the calculated paleolatitudes between western Lhasa and Qiangtang suggests a ∼ 9.3° discrepancy in latitude in 132–67 Ma. Instead of a spatial gap interpretation, we use the crustal shortening model of P. Song et al. ( 2022 ) to explain this. In this work, we provide robust data suggesting a latitude of ∼ 30.5 ± 5.0°N for western Qiangtang during the Early Cretaceous (ca. 110–100 Ma). We also compiled the available latitudinal data from western Tibet in combination with geological observations. We suggest Lhasa collided with Qiangtang during 132 million years ago in western Tibet. Introduction The evolution of the Tethyan domain during the formation and break‐up of Pangea involved various stages of the Wilson cycle spanning late Paleozoic‐early Cenozoic eras, characterized by the opening, growth, and closure of multiple oceans (i.e., the Paleo‐, Meso‐, and Neo‐Tethys oceans) (L. Ding et al., 2022 ; A. Yin & Harrison, 2000 ). The Meso‐Tethys ocean opened concurrently with the separation of the Cimmerian blocks (e.g., Qiangtang, Sibumasu) from southernly Gondwana (DeCelles et al., 2014 ; Metcalfe, 2013 ), and was then consumed by oceanic subduction beneath Qiangtang and /or Lhasa, accompanied by the rifting and northward drift of Lhasa toward northernly Eurasia (Kapp & Decelles, 2019 ). Plain Language Summary The collision of India and Asia caused intense tectonic deformation and hydrothermal alteration throughout the Tethyan Himalaya Terrane (THT), which resulted in the large‐scale remagnetization in the THT. The regional remagnetization of the THT can be used to constrain the India‐Asia collision process, on the premise that the time of remagnetization can be determined. Based on this assumption, we measured two representative Paleocene remagnetized components from Early Jurassic limestones in the Gyangze Basin in the east‐central THT. These remagnetized components, combined with non‐remagnetized components and remagnetization events recorded in the adjacent areas, suggest that the east‐central THT experienced three phases of regional remagnetization during 62.3–50.0 Ma. The first and second phases of remagnetization in the north‐central part of the east‐central THT occurred at the paleolatitude of 5.4 ± 0.9°N at 62.3–60.9 Ma and 10.3 ± 1.0°N–9.5 ± 1.1°N at 59.8–58.0 Ma, respectively. The third phase of remagnetization occurred in the southern part of the east‐central THT, at the paleolatitude of 10.9 ± 5.1°N at ∼ 50.0 Ma. The India‐Asia collision led to intense tectonic deformation and hydrothermal activity throughout the THT, resulting in large‐scale remagnetization of strata in the THT (Appel et al., 2012 ; Besse et al., 1984 ; Huang et al., 2015 , 2017a , 2017b ; Klootwijk & Bingham, 1980 ; Tong et al., 2008 ; Xu et al., 2022 ). The stage and timing of the India‐Asia collision during the entire suturing process could be generally consistent with that of the regional remagnetization in the THT. Thus, the spatio‐temporal process of the India‐Asia collision could be constrained by dating the acquisition times of remagnetized components from the Jurassic to Paleocene strata of the THT. Based on this concept, we conducted a paleomagnetic study on Early Jurassic limestones, which are known to be susceptible to remagnetization. Here, we obtained two representative Paleocene remagnetized components from the Gyangze Basin in the east‐central THT. Since the final suturing of the THT with Asia at ∼ 10°N during 59.8–58.0 Ma, the east‐central THT remained stationary until India collided with it at 10.9 ± 5.1°N at ∼ 50.0 Ma. Plain Language Summary The collision of India and Asia caused intense tectonic deformation and hydrothermal alteration throughout the Tethyan Himalaya Terrane (THT), which resulted in the large‐scale remagnetization in the THT. The regional remagnetization of the THT can be used to constrain the India‐Asia collision process, on the premise that the time of remagnetization can be determined. Based on this assumption, we measured two representative Paleocene remagnetized components from Early Jurassic limestones in the Gyangze Basin in the east‐central THT. These remagnetized components, combined with non‐remagnetized components and remagnetization events recorded in the adjacent areas, suggest that the east‐central THT experienced three phases of regional remagnetization during 62.3–50.0 Ma. The first and second phases of remagnetization in the north‐central part of the east‐central THT occurred at the paleolatitude of 5.4 ± 0.9°N at 62.3–60.9 Ma and 10.3 ± 1.0°N–9.5 ± 1.1°N at 59.8–58.0 Ma, respectively. The third phase of remagnetization occurred in the southern part of the east‐central THT, at the paleolatitude of 10.9 ± 5.1°N at ∼ 50.0 Ma. The paleomagnetic results reported by Yang et al. ( 1992 ) indicate that the Early Ordovician paleolatitude for the OT was ∼ 13°S; however, their Early Ordovician paleomagnetic results are derived from only 10 samples and they lack field tests. A new Early Ordovician paleomagnetic result was recently reported by Cao et al. ( 2021 ). This result also lacked field tests, but the characteristic remanent magnetizations are all reverse polarities and are consistent with the Moyero Reversed Polarity Superchron, which indicates the primary origin of the characteristic remanence. This result indicates that the OT was located at a low latitude near the equator during the Early Ordovician (Cao et al., 2021 ). Here we report the first Late Cambrian paleomagnetic results for the OT. These paleomagnetic results, combined with geological evidence, provide reliable constraints on the paleogeographic affinity of the terranes in the northern Tibetan Plateau, and the paleogeography of the Proto‐Tethys Ocean during the Late Cambrian. 2. The Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP) reported by Huang et al. Plain Language Summary The Proto‐Tethys Ocean underwent a complex process of collision and amalgamation of the terranes in the northern Tibetan Plateau during the Early Paleozoic. Unraveling the Early Paleozoic paleogeography of these terranes is important for understanding the evolution of the Proto‐Tethys Ocean and is critical for reconstructing the formation of East Asia. However, quantitative constraints on the Early Paleozoic paleogeographic position of the terranes in the northern Tibetan Plateau are limited. Plain Language Summary The tectono‐sedimentary evolution of the Cenozoic terrestrial sedimentary basins in the Tibetan Plateau was a long‐term response to Cenozoic continental collision and was critical for both constraining the amount of crustal shortening of the Asian continent and for paleogeographic reconstruction of the plateau. Nonetheless, the ages of the basins are controversial because of the discordance between radiometric dating results and paleontological ages. Siling Co is the geographic boundary between the Lunpola and Nima Basins, and the Niubao Formation is widely exposed on its northeastern margin, providing excellent research materials for studying the paleogeographic evolution of the plateau. Despite possible remagnetization, the dual‐polarity magnetization, hosted in different minerals and lithologies, likely represents a middle Permian remanence. New U‐Pb detrital zircon ages from sandstones further suggest the Lhasa Block was located along the northwestern margin of Australia prior to rifting. It is crucial to better resolve the spatio‐temporal context of the breakout of the Lhasa Block and the relationship between the YZO, the BNO and Neo‐Tethys, as the present spectrum of proposed scenarios have significantly different implications for our understanding of the geodynamic and paleo‐environmental evolution of the broader Tethyan region. Here we present the results of a paleomagnetic and geochronological investigation of volcanic and sedimentary rocks of the middle Permian Luobadui Formation from the Lhasa Block. Geological Setting and Sampling Upper Paleozoic strata are widely distributed in the Lhasa Block. Upper Carboniferous–lower Permian strata are characterized by glaciomarine diamictites that were then common across large areas of Gondwana, whereas middle to upper Permian strata are mainly distributed in the central part of the Lhasa Block, where they are characterized by marine sedimentary rocks, locally interbedded with volcanics (Figure 1a ). The latter include an early (middle Permian) phase of basaltic volcanism and a later (middle to late Permian) phase of intermediate to silicic volcanism (Geng et al., 2009 ). The most extensive exposure of the older volcanic phase, referred to as the Luobadui Formation, is located north of Luobadui village, Chundui Township, Lhunzhub County (Geng et al., 2009 ). The Luobadui Formation consists of a volcano‐sedimentary sequence, including marine carbonates and sandstones, interspersed with volcanic layers of basalt, basaltic breccia, tuff, and andesite. It is separated from the Tarim Block by the Altyn Tagh fault zone to the north, from the Songpan- Ganze Block by the East Kunlun fault zone to the southeast, and from the Kunlun Block by the Qimen Tagh fault zone to the south ( Fig. 1 b). Strata outcrops in the Qaidam Basin are mainly Cenozoic sediments. Outcrops of Pre-Cenozoic strata are limited to the western and northern margins, and outcrops of Carboniferous strata are limited to the basin margin. Major Upper Carboniferous deposits in the Qaidam Basin in- clude the Zhongwunongshan Group (C 2zh), the Zhabusagaxiu Forma- tion (C 2z) and Keluke Formation (C 2k). Lower Carboniferous deposits include the Huaitoutala Formation (C 1h) and Chengqianggou Formation (C1c). In the study area, outcropping rocks consist mainly of Paleozoic and Proterozoic strata ( Fig. 1c). Examples are the Cambrian Ou- longbuluke Formation, Ordovician Duoquanshan Formation, Lower Carboniferous Huaitoutala Formation, Upper Carboniferous Keluke Formation and Upper Carboniferous Zhabusagaxiu Formation. There are several NW-SE faults and left-lateral strike-slip faults in the study area ( Fig. 1c). The sampled locality lies at the northern margin of the Qaidam Block (Fig. 1). Paleomagnetic samples were collected from two

Late Carboniferous Zhabusagaxiu Formation. In total, we sampled 11 Early Carboniferous sites (106 samples) and 9 Late Carboniferous sites (74 samples) at the Shihuigou section (37.4 °N, 96.1 °E), and 9 Early Carboniferous sites (83 samples) at the Oulongbuluke section (37.2 °N, 96.7 °E) ( Figs. 2, 3, Table 1). Sampling was mainly conducted on limestone. In general, 10 samples were taken at each site, using a gasoline-powered drill, and were oriented using a magnetic compass. 3. It is separated from the Tarim Block by the Altyn Tagh fault zone to the north, from the Songpan- Ganze Block by the East Kunlun fault zone to the southeast, and from the Kunlun Block by the Qimen Tagh fault zone to the south ( Fig. 1 b). Strata outcrops in the Qaidam Basin are mainly Cenozoic sediments. Outcrops of Pre-Cenozoic strata are limited to the western and northern margins, and outcrops of Carboniferous strata are limited to the basin margin. Major Upper Carboniferous deposits in the Qaidam Basin in- clude the Zhongwunongshan Group (C 2zh), the Zhabusagaxiu Forma- tion (C 2z) and Keluke Formation (C 2k). Lower Carboniferous deposits include the Huaitoutala Formation (C 1h) and Chengqianggou Formation (C1c). In the study area, outcropping rocks consist mainly of Paleozoic and Proterozoic strata ( Fig. 1c). Examples are the Cambrian Ou- longbuluke Formation, Ordovician Duoquanshan Formation, Lower Carboniferous Huaitoutala Formation, Upper Carboniferous Keluke Formation and Upper Carboniferous Zhabusagaxiu Formation. There are several NW-SE faults and left-lateral strike-slip faults in the study area ( Fig. 1c). The sampled locality lies at the northern margin of the Qaidam Block (Fig. 1). Courtillot Abstract We have carried out a detailed magnetostratigraphic study of Tertiary sediments in the northern margin of the Qaidam Basin, northern Tibetan plateau. A total of 400 paleomagnetic samples (with an interval of about 2 m) were collected from the Shanggancaigou and Xiagancaigou Formations in the Hongsanhan section. Stepwise thermal demagnetization was used to isolate the magnetic components in these samples. A higher temperature component (HTC) was separated between 300 and 680 8C from most of samples. The basal parts of the sequences are mainly fine-grained and represent deposition centers lying at some distance from the uplifting mountains. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. Paleomagnetic constraints on the amount of displacement along the Altyn Tagh fault are difficult to establish because the fault’s easterly strike would require thousands of kilometers of offset in order to be resolvable by paleolatitude differences. One way around this problem is to use paleomagnetic rotations. First, if the Qaidam Basin rotated relative to the Tarim Basin, the relative motion must be mostly taken up by slip along the Altyn Tagh fault. Mesozoic to Recent Geology and Paleomagnetic Sampling [5] Sedimentary successions often crop out in the thrust packages exposed at the base of the mountains in central Asia. These, mainly Cenozoic, prograding sedimentary profiles are fairly monotonous throughout the region. The basal parts of the sequences are mainly fine-grained and represent deposition centers lying at some distance from the uplifting mountains. When crustal shortening and mountain building occurs, the mountains encroach upon the basins, which leads to progressively larger grain sizes reflecting increasingly proximal deposition. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. When crustal shortening and mountain building occurs, the mountains encroach upon the basins, which leads to progressively larger grain sizes reflecting increasingly proximal deposition. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. This is why we think that age con- straints solely based on facies correlation can have sig- nificant (10 – 20 Myr) errors. Mesozoic to Recent Geology and Paleomagnetic Sampling [5] Sedimentary successions often crop out in the thrust packages exposed at the base of the mountains in central Asia. Samples were mainly collected from Jurassic to Neogene siltstones and sandstones. In most cases stepwise thermal demagnetization unblocks low and high temperature components carried by magnetite and hematite. The ten overall mean directions display a complex pattern of vertical-axis block rotations that are compatible with a tectonic model of clockwise rotation of the Qaidam Basin and concomitant left-lateral slip on the Altyn Tagh fault. Paleomagnetic constraints on the amount of displacement along the Altyn Tagh fault are difficult to establish because the fault’s easterly strike would require thousands of kilometers of offset in order to be resolvable by paleolatitude differences. One way around this problem is to use paleomagnetic rotations. First, if the Qaidam Basin rotated relative to the Tarim Basin, the relative motion must be mostly taken up by slip along the Altyn Tagh fault. Second, one can sample time- progressive sequences to determine when (or if) a partic- ular block had (or had not) rotated. A paleomagnetic study along the Altyn Tagh fault by Rumelhar

zes reflecting increasingly proximal deposition. We have observed these coarsening-upward sedimentary sequences all around the margin of the Tarim Basin, on both sides of the Tian Shan and within the Qaidam Basin; however, they are not necessarily coeval, even within a few millions of years. This is why we think that age con- straints solely based on facies correlation can have sig- nificant (10 – 20 Myr) errors. Pre-Cenozoic sediments are generally distinct from Cenozoic sediments and are fairly repetitive throughout central Asia. Cretaceous sediments are generally red to brick red, whereas Upper Jurassic red beds are interbedded with green sandstones and siltstones. All paleomagnetic specimens underwent either stepwise thermal demagnetization up to 580 °C using an ASC- TD 48 furnace with an internal residualﬁeld less than 10 nT or stepwise alternatingﬁeld demagnetization up to 120 mT using a D-2000 alternatingﬁeld demagnetizer. Thermal demagnetization steps were set to 50 °C below 450 °C and shifted to 30– 10 °C above 450 °C; alternating ﬁeld intervals were set to 2.5– 5 mT below 30 mT and changed to 10 mT above 30 mT. The paleomagnetic specimens with strong natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensity were measured using a JR-6A spinner magnetometer, and those with weak NRM intensity were measured using a 2G-755-4K cryogenic magnetometer. To better constrain the Jurassic and Cretaceous paleogeographic position of the Tethyan Himalaya and the breakup of eastern Gondwana, a combined paleomagnetic and geochronological study was performed on the Zhela and Weimei Formations lava ﬂows, dated at ~138 – 135 Ma, in the Luozha area of the eastern Tethyan Himalaya. Both positive fold and reversal tests together with a maximum grouping at 100% unfolding indicate that the characteristic remanent magnetization directions are primary magnetizations acquired before folding. The tilt-corrected directions yielded a paleopole at 0.9°N, 293.4°E with A 95 = 7.0° and a corresponding paleolatitude of 53.5°S ± 7.0°S for the Luozha sampling area (28.9°N, 91.3°E), validating that the original erupted position of the Zhela and Weimei Formations lava ﬂows was located in the center of the Kerguelen mantle plume. Our new results, together with the published paleomagnetic, geochronological, and geochemical results, demonstrate that the Comei-Bunbury large igneous province originated from the Kerguelen mantle plume. ute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Guangzhou, China, 4Beijing SHRIMP Center, Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Beijing, China Abstract The breakup of eastern Gondwana is among the hottest topics in the Earth sciences because of its effect on global climate during the Jurassic-Cretaceous, its in ﬂuence on the evolution of life, and its importance to paleogeographic reconstruction. To better constrain the Jurassic and Cretaceous paleogeographic position of the Tethyan Himalaya and the breakup of eastern Gondwana, a combined paleomagnetic and geochronological study was performed on the Zhela and Weimei Formations lava ﬂows, dated at ~138 – 135 Ma, in the Luozha area of the eastern Tethyan Himalaya. Both positive fold and reversal tests together with a maximum grouping at 100% unfolding indicate that the characteristic remanent magnetization directions are primary magnetizations acquired before folding. The tilt-corrected directions yielded a paleopole at 0.9°N, 293.4°E with A 95 = 7.0° and a corresponding paleolatitude of 53.5°S ± 7.0°S for the Luozha sampling area (28.9°N, 91.3°E), validating that the original erupted position of the Zhela and Weimei Formations lava ﬂows was located in the center of the Kerguelen mantle plume. a combined paleomagnetic and geochronological study was performed on the Zhela and Weimei Formations lava ﬂows, dated at ~138 – 135 Ma, in the Luozha area of the eastern Tethyan Himalaya. Both positive fold and reversal tests together with a maximum grouping at 100% unfolding indicate that the characteristic remanent magnetization directions are primary magnetizations acquired before folding. The tilt-corrected directions yielded a paleopole at 0.9°N, 293.4°E with A 95 = 7.0° and a corresponding paleolatitude of 53.5°S ± 7.0°S for the Luozha sampling area (28.9°N, 91.3°E), validating that the original erupted position of the Zhela and Weimei Formations lava ﬂows was located in the center of the Kerguelen mantle plume. Our new results, together with the published paleomagnetic, geochronological, and geochemical results, demonstrate that the Comei-Bunbury large igneous province originated from the Kerguelen mantle plume. Introduction Large igneous provinces (LIPs) are magmatic provinces that cover areas greater than 100,000 km 2, contain igneous volumes exceeding 100,000 km 3, and are usually characterized by an intense eruptive pulse(s) of short duration ( –5 Myr)

al rela- tionship with the KMP. Considering that (1) some published latest Jurassic and Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic data from the TH lack robust ﬁeld tests to question the reliability of the data ( Klootwijk and Bingham, 1980; Zhu et al., 1981; Patzelt et al., 1996; Li et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2015 ); and (2) although these Jurassic and Cre- taceous igneous rocks have an overall similarity in geochemical characteristics to the KMP (e.g., Zhu et al., 2007, 2008; Shi et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2022 ), the spatial relationship of these latest Jurassic and Early Cretaceous igneous rocks to the KMP is an essential prerequisite for understanding the causal link between the eastern Gondwana breakup and the KMP, additional reliable latest Jurassic and Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic data- sets with well-established ages constraint from the TH are still required to address the aforementioned issues. In this study, we present an analysis of paleomagnetic data on the Zhela Formation (Fm.) basalts and sandstones in the Taga area of the eastern TH. The new results allow us to constrain the pale- ogeography of the TH during the latest Jurassic to Early Cretaceous and thus provide a better understanding of the causal link between the CBLIP and the KMP. 2. Introduction The geomagnetic field, produced by thermo-chemical convection of an electrically conducting fluid in Earth's outer core, experienced significant changes in its rate of polarity reversals throughout geologic times. In particular, two end-member polarity regimes have been identified during the Phanerozoic (e.g., Gallet & Pavlov, 2016). On the one hand, three superchrons—the Cretaceous Normal Superchron (CNS, 84–121 Ma), the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (267–318 Ma) and the Ordovician Reverse Superchron (463–485 Ma)—are defined as prolonged periods with stable polarity (e.g., Ogg, 2020; Pavlov & Gallet, 2005). On the other, two hyperactivity events, with more than 10 reversals per million year, were hypothesized during the Middle Jurassic (155–171 Ma; e.g., Tivey et al., 2006; Tominaga et al., 2008

Most VGPs remain in the northern hemisphere (positive latitudes) at high latitudes ( > 60 ◦ ), with a few migrating to the southern hemisphere but only reaching medium lati - tudes, compatible with an excursion and not a complete reversal of the geomagnetic field. However, at the base of sections 1 to 3 , the variability of the VGPs suggests a recovering field from a reversal. The topmost sections, 6 and 7, exhibit different behavior than the others, with their VGPs at medium latitudes in the base and a complete reversal on the top of the sequences between elevations 772 – 774 m. The reversed magne - tization component is of primary origin and remains stable during de - magnetizations up to 80 mT or 600 ◦ C. This reversed field was probably imparted as a soft secondary component in a few samples of sections 1 and 2 , as mentioned before and seen in Figs. 3 and 5 . On the stereogram of Fig. 8 , the distribution of the VGPs calculated after the inclination correction shows a tight cluster near the geographic pole corresponding mainly to the results from sections 1 to 5 and a higher dispersion of data from sections 6 and 7. Most of these VGPs plot outside the polar cap delimited by the parallel 45 ◦ , compatible with a varying field as was the field at the end of the Cretaceous Normal Superchron (CNS), which lasted from ~126 to 84 Ma ( He et al., 2012 ). Notably, the Uberaba Formation, which occupies a restricted area in the northeastern portion of the basin ( Fig. 1 ), is in contact with the Serra Geral basalts. Despite this, its depositional characteristics indicate contributions from the Late Cretaceous Alto Paranaiba alkaline volcanism to the north ( Ferreira Júnior and Gomes, 1999 ). Previous magnetostratigraphic research on the Uberaba Formation placed it in the Campanian-Maastrichtian ( Tamrat et al., 2002 ), and the authors identified some polarity intervals loosely correlated with the geomagnetic polarity time scale. However, the rough data was never fully published, and no paleomagnetic pole was calculated. Here, we will reanalyze the previously studied Uberaba sections to verify the findings and potentially provide a more accurate age for the Uberaba Formation. n the Bauru Group, was deposited over the Early Cretaceous volcanic rocks of the Paran ´a Basin in southern Brazil. It occupies a restricted northeastern area of the basin surrounding the homonymous city. Recent works on stratigraphy and paleontology indicate a Campanian age, a novel finding that challenges the previously held belief of a Cenomanian age based on dinosaur bones. Paleomagnetic work on seven sections of the Uberaba formation has resulted in the calculation of a paleo - magnetic pole at 82.2 ◦ S 350.8 ◦ E (N = 89; k = 23; A 95 = 3.2 ◦ ) after correcting for the shallowing of the magnetic inclination caused by overload. The formation is dated to ~73 Ma (Campanian) age based on magnetostrati - graphic data and comparisons with other Late Cretaceous poles. The area stayed as a highland until the tectonic events related to the northward emplacement of the alkaline provinces. The Cuojiangding Group and the Xigaze Group strata were deformed by kilometer-scale synclinal folds, which are intersected by east-west trending Gangdese thrust struc- tures. The Gangdese thrust fault cut and placed the Xigaze and Cuojiangding Groups in the hanging wall and transported them southward over the Late Eocene-Miocene conglomerates 14,24,25. The timing of slip on the Gangdese thrust has been inferred between 30 and 23 Ma 25. The Late Eocene-Miocene conglomerates were not folded. Thus, folding must have occurred during the Eocene, enab- ling a palaeomagnetic fold test on the age of magnetization. In the area we studied, the Quxia Formation is ,80 m thick and is dominated by conglomerates with sandstone intercalations. The Gyalaze Formation is .120 m thick and composed of gray to dark gray foraminiferal sandy limestone and lithic sandstone. Well-lithified volcanic tuff layers occur near the middle part of the Gyalaze Formation, affording radiometric dates to further constrain the age of formation (54.8 60.7 Ma, Dr. Xiumian Hu, personal communication). (2022) suggested that the Lhasa terrane in the Late Cretaceous was located at ~ 11-15 ◦ N in a WNW-ESE orientation. Notably, its shape during the early Eocene remains poorly understood. Finally, most of the previous results were from the interior part of the Lhasa terrane; only paleomagnetic studies from the Xigaze forearc basin can truly represent the southern margin of Asia before the India – Asia collision and do not need to consider potential crustal shortening within the Lhasa terrane ( Meng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2022 ). More reliable paleomagnetic results from the Xigaze forearc basin would be useful for providing further constraints on the paleogeography of the southern margin of the Lhasa terrane during the late Paleocene. Therefore, we conducted paleomagnetic studies on the upper Paleocene (Thanetian stage) Jialazi Formation within the Xigaze forearc basin. 2. Geological setting and sampling The Tibetan Plateau presents a complex orogenic collage primarily composed of distinct tectonic units arranged from north to south, including the Songpan – Ganze terrane, Qiangtang terrane, Lhasa terrane, and Himalayas ( Yin and Harrison, 2000 ) ( Fig. 1 a). These units are delineated by prominent sut

thys, respectively ( Gehrels et al., 2011; Metcalfe, 2013 ). The Lhasa terrane is segmented into southern and northern subterranes ( Wang et al., 2022 ), with the Gangdese (or Transhimalayan) magmatic arc prevailing in the southern section, primarily consisting of Mesozoic to Eocene intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019 ). To the south of the Lhasa terrane, the IYS features Xigaze forearc basin (XFB) and the Xigaze accretionary complex, which include ophiolites and m ´elanges ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019; Wang et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2013 ). The Xigaze ophiolite, often in tectonic contact with forearc sediments, is posited as the basement for the forearc strata ( Huang et al., 2015 ). Stretching more than 500 km from Renbu in the east to Zhongba in the west, the XFB extends along the Yarlung Zangbo River in an east – west orientation ( Wang et al., 2012 ). Isolated remnants of forearc sediments are sporadically found in the Zanda area ( Sun et al., 2018 ). The XFB, dating from the Early Cretaceous to the Eocene, is exposed as an east – west trending syncline with a westward inclination ( Metcalf and Kapp, 2019 ). (2022) suggested that the Lhasa terrane in the Late Cretaceous was located at ~ 11-15 ◦ N in a WNW-ESE orientation. Notably, its shape during the early Eocene remains poorly understood. Finally, most of the previous results were from the interior part of the Lhasa terrane; only paleomagnetic studies from the Xigaze forearc basin can truly represent the southern margin of Asia before the India – Asia collision and do not need to consider potential crustal shortening within the Lhasa terrane ( Meng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2022 ). More reliable paleomagnetic results from the Xigaze forearc basin would be useful for providing further constraints on the paleogeography of the southern margin of the Lhasa terrane during the late Paleocene. Therefore, we conducted paleomagnetic studies on the upper Paleocene (Thanetian stage) Jialazi Formation within the Xigaze forearc basin. 2. Geological setting and sampling The Tibetan Plateau presents a complex orogenic collage primarily composed of distinct tectonic units arranged from north to south, including the Songpan – Ganze terrane, Qiangtang terrane, Lhasa terrane, and Himalayas ( Yin and Harrison, 2000 ) ( Fig. 1 a). These units are delineated by prominent sut

thys, respectively ( Gehrels et al., 2011; Metcalfe, 2013 ). The Lhasa terrane is segmented into southern and northern subterranes ( Wang et al., 2022 ), with the Gangdese (or Transhimalayan) magmatic arc prevailing in the southern section, primarily consisting of Mesozoic to Eocene intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019 ). To the south of the Lhasa terrane, the IYS features Xigaze forearc basin (XFB) and the Xigaze accretionary complex, which include ophiolites and m ´elanges ( Kapp and DeCelles, 2019; Wang et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2013 ). The Xigaze ophiolite, often in tectonic contact with forearc sediments, is posited as the basement for the forearc strata ( Huang et al., 2015 ). Stretching more than 500 km from Renbu in the east to Zhongba in the west, the XFB extends along the Yarlung Zangbo River in an east – west orientation ( Wang et al., 2012 ). Isolated remnants of forearc sediments are sporadically found in the Zanda area ( Sun et al., 2018 ). The XFB, dating from the Early Cretaceous to the Eocene, is exposed as an east – west trending syncline with a westward inclination ( Metcalf and Kapp, 2019 ). However, estimates of Greater India extent have significant discrepancies in the Early Cretaceous. Magnetic mineralogy The magnetic properties of samples from the sections and cores range from hard to soft coercivity behaviour, with high coercivity minerals (haematite, goethite) seen by the non-saturation at 300 mT IRM fields ( Fig. 9 a,e), and remanent coercivity (Hcr) > 200 mT (SI Fig. S8). At Backside Beck the red-samples from the Hebblethwaite Mbr, and some non-red samples from the Browgill Fm have > 80% of IRM acquisition above 200 mT and Hcr > 280 mT ( Fig. 9 a). Similar behaviour is seen to dominate the reddish lithologies from Hillend Farm and Buttington Quarry ( Fig. 9 e). The hard ferrimagnetic mineral in most of these sam - ples is haematite as shown by the resistance of the NRM to thermal demagnetisation (see later). Fig. 6. Detailed magnetic and organic matter car

Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Magnetic mineralogy The magnetic properties of samples from the sections and cores range from hard to soft coercivity behaviour, with high coercivity minerals (haematite, goethite) seen by the non-saturation at 300 mT IRM fields ( Fig. 9 a,e), and remanent coercivity (Hcr) > 200 mT (SI Fig. S8). Similar behaviour is seen to dominate the reddish lithologies from Hillend Farm and Buttington Quarry ( Fig. 9 e). Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Magnetic results 4.1. Magnetic mineralogy The magnetic properties of samples from the sections and cores range from hard to soft coercivity behaviour, with high coercivity minerals (haematite, goethite) seen by the non-saturation at 300 mT IRM fields ( Fig. 9 a,e), and remanent coercivity (Hcr) > 200 mT (SI Fig. S8). At Backside Beck the red-samples from the Hebblethwaite Mbr, and some non-red samples from the Browgill Fm have > 80% of IRM acquisition above 200 mT and Hcr > 280 mT ( Fig. 9 a). Similar behaviour is seen to dominate the reddish lithologies from Hillend Farm and Buttington Quarry ( Fig. 9 e). The hard ferrimagnetic mineral in most of these sam - ples is haematite as shown by the resistance of the NRM to thermal demagnetisation (see later). Fig. 6. Detailed magnetic and organic matter car

the Silurian at Bardo Stawy (Zbra Fm), Grabowiec-6, Core-A and grey lithologies at Butting - ton Quarry have some of the softest behaviour (H cr < 35 mT; SI Fig. s8), but with some of these also having 10 – 20% IRM acquisition above 200 mT ( Fig. 9 b,d,e). Behaviours intermediate between these hard and soft end members are found at Backside Beck and Bardo Stawy (Rembow Fm; Fig. 9 a,b). The relative consistency of the Hcr and IRM 1T / χ ARM values in those samples with soft coercivity behaviour, suggest a similar miner - alogy in most of the sections and cores. Using the data in Peters and Dekkers (2003) suggests this is most likely magnetite, with magnetic particle sizes < 0.1 μ m in size (SI Fig. S8). 4.2. Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . Magnetic mineralogy The magnetic properties of samples from the sections and cores range from hard to soft coercivity behaviour, with high coercivity minerals (haematite, goethite) seen by the non-saturation at 300 mT IRM fields ( Fig. 9 a,e), and remanent coercivity (Hcr) > 200 mT (SI Fig. S8). Similar behaviour is seen to dominate the reddish lithologies from Hillend Farm and Buttington Quarry ( Fig. 9 e). Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Conclusions Our magnetostratigraphic data allows the construction of the first geomagnetic polarity chronostratigraphic scale for the ca.10.4 Myr of the Llandovery, ranging into the earliest Wenlock. This is defined using polarity data from six sections, a dataset supported by fold and reversal tests, indicating the primary nature of the magnetisations, which is carried by variable mixtures of both haematite and magnetite. At the Backside Beck section, directional data is consistent with previous palaeomagnetic data from the area. We construct a correlation and age framework onto which these magnetostratigraphic datasets are linked, using: a) existing graptolite biostratigraphy b) correlations using carbon isotope changes, and c) magnetic susceptibility data for within UK sec - tion correlations . The polarity boundaries are generally rather loosely tied to the graptolite biozones for most of this interval, and will require more work to improve cross-calibration. Sample acquisition, preparation, measurement and rock magnetic analysis 3.1. Acquisition, preparation, measurement and demagnetization All samples were obtained as oriented cores in the field using stan - dard methods. In the Pacific Northwest Paleomagnetism Laboratory at the Western Washington University, the 2.5 cm in diameters cores were sliced into specimens 2.2 cm in length. Remanent magnetization was measured with a 2G Enterprise model 755 three-axis DC-SQUID magnetometer in a magnetically shielded room, which has an internal field of less than 350 nT. Progressive thermal demagnetization was employed to reveal components of Natural Remanent Magnetization (NRM) of specimens using the ASC model TD48 furnace. Progressive alternating field (a.f.) demagnetization used an ASC D-2000 unit with peak fields of 200 mT. A total of 345 specimens, 190 from Upper Triassic and 155 from Middle Jurassic formations, were demagnetized. Samples that were suspected to have magnetite as their main remanence carrier were demagnetized using a.f., which was generally ineffective, and at best a large p

rge portion of NRM (generally > 50%) remained after a.f. demagneti - zation. At least one specimen per layer was selected for pilot thermal demagnetization with temperature steps of 50 – 100 ◦ C below 500 ◦ C, 10 – 30 ◦ C between 500 ◦ and 630 ◦ or 650 ◦ C, and 3 – 10 ◦ C above 650 ◦ C. After this revealed the general demagnetization behavior of each set, most of the specimens were thermally cleaned at larger intervals below 500 ◦ C, 30 – 40 ◦ C steps up to 600 ◦ or 630 ◦ C, and very small steps (3 – 10 ◦ C) for temperatures above 630 ◦ C. In most samples, it appeared that hematite is the main carrier of the remanence, and unblocking temperature ranges above 650 ◦ C were used to reveal the Characteristic Remanent Magnetization (ChRM) compo - nent of specimens. Linear demagnetization paths (at high unblocking temperature ranges) were quantified with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of Kirschvink (1980) , while the great-circle (GC) fits ( McFadden and McElhinny, 1988 ) were employed for non-linear paths. To not bias directions by possible relatively high-temperature overprints, unan - chored line-fits were used for most specimens. For those few specimens whose linear path clearly trended toward the origin, line-fits were anchored to the origin. Mean paleomagnetic directions

The APWP from coeval NA sedimentary rocks define a lower-latitude, more continuous path. The discrepancy between the two paths has been attributed to inclination error (IE) from deposition and compaction of the sediments. The age of the Tiaojishan Formation volcanics was recently dated from 153 Ma to 161 Ma by U –Pb and 40Ar–39Ar. A total of 154 samples from 16 sites within the Tiaojishan Formation were collected. Detailed stepwise thermal demagnetization allows us to isolate two components from 77 oriented drill-core samples. A low-temperature component identi ﬁed in most samples falls close to the present local Earth ﬁeld direction. Characteristic remanent directions obtained from high-temperature pass-reversal test yield a pole position at 240.3°E, 59.9°N with α95 = 6.8°. Combined with coeval paleopoles obtained from the Siberia Block (SIB), these results show a signi ﬁcant paleolatitude displacement between the NCB and SIB, which indicates that the Mongol –Okhotsk Ocean was still open with ~ 3000 km width in its eastern part at ca. 155 Ma. © 2011 Elsevier B.V. Fields of 2.4 T, 0.4 T and 0.12 T were applied along the Z, Y and X axes of the specimens, respectively. Then, stepwise thermal demagnetization up to 680°C was performed. IRM were measured using the IM-10 impulse magnetizer and the JR-6 magnetometer. All samples were subsequently subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization up to 600 °C or 680°C in 12 –14 steps using an ASC- Scientiﬁc TD-48 thermal demagnetizer with an interval residual ﬁeld lower than 10 nT. The age of the Tiaojishan Formation volcanics was recently dated from 153 Ma to 161 Ma by U –Pb and 40Ar–39Ar. A total of 154 samples from 16 sites within the Tiaojishan Formation were collected. Detailed stepwise thermal demagnetization allows us to isolate two components from 77 oriented drill-core samples. A low-temperature component identi ﬁed in most samples falls close to the present local Earth ﬁeld direction. Characteristic remanent directions obtained from high-temperature pass-reversal test yield a pole position at 240.3°E, 59.9°N with α95 = 6.8°. Geological setting and paleomagnetic sampling The Chengde basin is geologically located in the southern margin of the Yanshan Belt (YSB), itself located at the northern margin of the NCB ( Fig. 1 ; Davis et al., 2001; Zhao, 1990 ). To the north, the Xing- Meng suture (Suolon suture) indicates a ﬁnal closure of the Paleo- Asian ocean and the collision between the NCB and AMU during the Permian (Badarch et al., 2002; Li, 2006; Xiao et al., 2004; Yin and Nie, 1996). The YSB experienced vertical movements accompanied by intense deformation during the Mesozoic, including multiple generations of folds, thrusts and extensional faults (Davis et al., 2001; Zhao, 1990). In the Early Jurassic, a series of rift basins bounded by normal faulting were developed on the amalgamated NCB and AMU ( Darby et al., 2001; Meng, 2003; Zhao et al., 2002 ). From Early Jurassic to Early Cretaceous, extensive terrestrial volcanic and clastic sediments were deposited in these fault-related rift basins. These volcanic rocks, varying from ma ﬁc to intermediate- acid in composition, were genetically related to the process of lithospheric replacement beneath the NCB ( Zhang et al., 2003 ). Thermal demagnetization isolated a high-temperature magnetization component with unblocking temperatures of 500–580 ◦C from ﬁve sites of the Early Jurassic Y ongdingzhuang Formation in the Datong area. Palaeomagnetic directions from the ﬁve sites yielded a positive fold test at the 95 per cent conﬁdence level. These directions combined together with previously reported ones give a new Early Jurassic mean direction ( D = 358.0 ◦, I = 50.6◦, α95 = 4.4◦) and corresponding palaeomagnetic pole (81.5◦N, 302.5◦E, A95 = 5.5◦). Key words: Mesozoic, North China Block, palaeomagnetism, tectonics. 1 INTRODUCTION The North China Block and the South China Block are the major tectonic blocks forming East Asia (Fig. 1). The two blocks were located in distinct positions from each other through Precambrian– Palaeozoic times and were welded through a collision process in Early Mesozoic times. The collision of the North and South China Blocks is recognized by metamorphic belts observed between the two blocks. The Dabie Belt and the Sulu Belt that bound the two blocks yield coesite-bearing ultrahigh-pressure metamorphic rocks (Okay & S¸ eng¨or 1992). The Tan-Lu Fault also marks the bound- ary between the North and South China Blocks. This fault, to the north of the Dabie Belt and to the south of the Sulu Belt, marks the biogeographical and lithological boundary between the two blocks (Kobayashi 1967). Permian and Early Mesozoic palaeomagnetic data sets from the North and South China Blocks suggest that the two blocks su- tured following a scissor-like collision process (Zhao & Coe 1987). The North and South China Blocks experienced counterclockwise and clockwise rotations during the welding event, respectively. The Nor

e North China Block with respect to the South China Block during the welding event. At present, the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic representa- tive poles for the North China Block are based on palaeomagnetic data from a small number of studies (Y ang et al. 1991, 1992) that come from a single locality within the block (Ordos Basin, Fig. 1). The palaeomagnetic data of these important time periods have not been improved over the last decade. Attempts to accumulate reliable Triassic and Jurassic data have been thwarted by remagnetizations and lack of outcrops with good structural conditions to perform fold tests. As seen in the Early Jurassic demagnetization results of Y anget al. (1992), even successful palaeomagnetic works have encountered difﬁculties in isolating a high-ﬁdelity record of geo- magnetic ﬁeld directions in the North China Block, and a further study needs to be undertaken in order to contribute toward establish- ing representative Triassic and Jurassic poles for the North China Block. In this paper we present new palaeomagnetic results from Late Triassic and Early Jurassic rocks in the North China Block. This paper includes the ﬁrst report of a positive fold test for Early Jurassic rocks in the North China Block and improves the representative pole position in the Early Jurassic.

Received 2005 March 2; in original form 2004 February 2 SUMMARY Middle Triassic red-purple sandstones were sampled at four localities in the northeastern part of the South China Block (SCB) to detect regional deformational features. Most of the samples gave a characteristic remanent magnetization with unblocking temperatures up to 680 ◦C. The Middle Triassic Badong Forma- tion is about 1087 m thick and consists of four different stratigraphic members (BGMRHB 1990). The lower two members have been as- signed to an Anisian age and the upper two members to a Ladinian age. As shown in Fig. 2(a), red-purple sandstones of all four mem- bers were sampled from 22 sites (206 samples) 40 km southwest of Nanzhang County (31.5 ◦N, 111.7◦E). The strata dip nearly north- or southward and the angle of dip ranges between 16◦ and 44◦. Nine out of 22 sites (HB49–HB57) were sampled from both limbs of an anticline. 2.2 The Tongling area The M

Received 2005 March 2; in original form 2004 February 2 SUMMARY Middle Triassic red-purple sandstones were sampled at four localities in the northeastern part of the South China Block (SCB) to detect regional deformational features. Most of the samples gave a characteristic remanent magnetization with unblocking temperatures up to 680 ◦C. In the laboratory, 2.2 cm long specimens were sliced from each sample. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of each spec- imen was measured using a cryogenic magnetometer (2G Enter- prises) at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory, Kobe University. All spec- imens were subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization using a Natsuhara TDS-1 thermal demagnetizer. The residual ﬁeld of this demagnetizer was less than 5 nT. The bulk magnetic susceptibility of each specimen was measured after each demagnetization step in order to monitor magnetic mineralogical alteration during progressive heat- ing. The study provides reliable Late Carboniferous-Permian paleomagnetic directions, in an area where paleomagnetic studies are scarce. The main characteristic component in both rock types shows a SSE direction with a shallow inclination and a dominant reverse polarity. The magnetic carriers, both in the volcanic rocks and the red beds, are magnetite and hematite. The main component is interpreted as a primary magnetization of Permian age in the red beds; in the Late Carboniferous volcanic rocks, the main component likely represents primary magnetization or early remagne - tization. These results are consistent with the poles for the Iberian plate during the Permian and indicate an absence of regional vertical axis rotations for the Orri nappe, in whose hanging wall the Cadí Basin was trans - ported southwards during the Pyrenean orogeny. 1. The Lower Red Unit (LRU) is mainly composed of siltstones, sandstones, acidic tuffs and red volca - niclastic microconglomerates. In the Cadí Basin, these lithologies interfinger with pyroclastic rocks that contain ignimbrites and inter - bedded banded rhyolites. Finally, the Upper Red Unit (URU) contains red conglomerates, sandstones, and siltstones ( Fig. 1 G) with carbonate nodules, and lacustrine deposits. These rocks are arranged in two se - quences, with interbedded volcanic bodies at the bottom. Mafic minerals and plagioclases in the volcanic series are replaced by opaque minerals, chlorite, ferromagnesian silicates, carbonates and sericite ( Gisbert, 1981 ; Bixel, 1984 ). Radiometric dating of extrusive rocks of the GU in the Cadí Basin yielded Late Carboniferous ages, including 304.0 ± 1.5 Ma (andesite) and 300.4 ± 1.4 Ma (ignimbrite) ( Pereira et al., 2014 ). 3. Stepwise thermal demagnetization is performed and vector analysis is used to isolate magnetic components, which illustrates a single magnetic co mponent or double magnetic compone nts. Compared with the inclination of the Early Cretaceous from red beds of north Tarim, the contemporary inclination of southwest Tarim is 10.0°±7.8° sharper, but it is still 8.1 ° ±8.9°, shallower than that of Early Cretaceous bas alts in southwest Tarim. Natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) were measured with 2-G Enterprises cryogenic magnetometer. At least one specimen from each sample was subjected to stepwise thermal demagneti- zation procedure up to 690 ◦C using Natsuhara TDS-1 thermal demagnetizer (with a residual ﬁeld of less than 5 nT). The Mavillette gabbro sill intruded ca. 440–430 Myr old bimodal rift-related metavolcanic and metasedimentary rocks of the White Rock Formation in the Silurian – Devonian Rockville Notch Group. The 426.4 6 2.0 Ma Mavillette gabbro age is notably younger than the ca. 440 Ma magmatism, but is part of a geochemically de ﬁned suite of within-plate sills and volcanic rocks of the Rockville Notch Group with ages as young as Early Devonian. Paleomagnetic investigation of 13 sites distributed along the Neoacadian (ca. 390 Ma) synclinal limbs of the Mavillette sill reveal magnetization directions that fail a fold test and therefore postdate Silurian emplacement of the gabbro.
